statement: Given two commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.
heath_proof: Let the two given commensurable magnitudes be AB, CD of which AB is the less; thus it is required to find the greatest common measure of AB, CD. Now the magnitude AB either measures CD or it does not. If then it measures it—and it measures itself also— AB is a common measure of AB, CD. And it is manifest that it is also the greatest; for a greater magnitude than the magnitude AB will not measure AB. Next, let AB not measure CD. Then, if the less be continually subtracted in turn from the greater, that which is left over will sometime measure the one before it, because AB, CD are not incommensurable; [cf. X. 2] let AB, measuring ED, leave EC less than itself, let EC, measuring FB, leave AF less than itself, and let AF measure CE. Since, then, AF measures CE, while CE measures FB, therefore AF will also measure FB. But it measures itself also; therefore AF will also measure the whole AB. But AB measures DE; therefore AF will also measure ED. But it measures CE also; therefore it also measures the whole CD. Therefore AF is a common measure of AB, CD. I say next that it is also the greatest. For, if not, there will be some magnitude greater than AF which will measure AB, CD. Let it be G. Since then G measures AB, while AB measures ED, therefore G will also measure ED. But it measures the whole CD also; therefore G will also measure the remainder CE. But CE measures FB; therefore G will also measure FB. But it measures the whole AB also, and it will therefore measure the remainder AF, the greater the less: which is impossible. Therefore no magnitude greater than AF will measure AB, CD; therefore AF is the greatest common measure of AB, CD. Therefore the greatest common measure of the two given commensurable magnitudes AB, CD has been found.
ai_proof_text:
10.3
**Statement:** Given two commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let AB, CD be the two given commensurable magnitudes, and let AB be the less of them (if they are equal, each measures the other, and the argument of Steps 2–3 applies without change). Since AB, CD are commensurable, there is some magnitude which measures both of them (D10.1.1); it is required to find the greatest such magnitude. Now either AB measures CD, or it does not.

**Step 2.** First let AB measure CD. Since AB also measures itself, AB is a common measure of AB and CD.

**Step 3.** AB is moreover the greatest common measure. For no magnitude greater than AB can measure AB: a magnitude which measures another is contained in it a whole number of times, and so is either equal to it or a part of it (D5.1), and a part is less than the whole (CN5); thus any magnitude measuring AB is not greater than AB. Hence no magnitude greater than AB measures both AB and CD, and AB is the greatest common measure required.

**Step 4.** Next let AB not measure CD. Let the less be continually subtracted in turn from the greater: AB from CD as many times as possible, then the remainder from AB as many times as possible, and so on. It cannot happen that every remainder fails to measure the one before it; for then, by 10.2, AB and CD would be incommensurable, whereas they are commensurable (D10.1.1). Therefore at some stage a remainder measures the one before it. For definiteness let this happen at the third stage (the reasoning is identical however many stages are required): let AB, measuring ED, leave EC less than itself; let EC, measuring FB, leave AF less than itself; and let AF measure CE. Then CD is made up of CE and ED, and AB is made up of AF and FB.

**Step 5.** Since AF measures CE, and CE measures FB, AF also measures FB; for FB is made up of magnitudes each equal to CE, and each of these is made up of magnitudes each equal to AF.

**Step 6.** AF measures FB (Step 5) and also measures itself, AF; hence AF measures the whole AB, since the magnitudes equal to AF which make up FB, together with AF itself, make up AB.

**Step 7.** AF measures AB (Step 6), and AB measures ED; hence, as in Step 5, AF measures ED. But AF also measures CE (Step 4); hence AF measures the whole CD, which is made up of CE and ED.

**Step 8.** Therefore AF measures both AB and CD, and is a common measure of them.

**Step 9.** I say that AF is also the greatest common measure. For, if not, let G be a magnitude greater than AF which measures both AB and CD. Since G measures AB, and AB measures ED, G measures ED (as in Step 5). But G also measures the whole CD; therefore G measures the remainder CE as well, since when the magnitudes equal to G which make up ED are taken away from those which make up CD, those which are left make up CE. Again, since G measures CE, and CE measures FB, G measures FB; and G measures the whole AB; therefore, in the same way, G measures the remainder AF. Thus G, which is greater than AF, measures AF; but this is impossible, for a magnitude measuring AF is either equal to AF or a part of AF (D5.1), and hence not greater than AF (CN5).

**Step 10.** Therefore no magnitude greater than AF measures both AB and CD; and AF, which measures both, is their greatest common measure. Thus, given two commensurable magnitudes AB, CD, their greatest common measure has been found. Q.E.F.

**Step 11.** (Corollary.) The hypothesis G > AF was used in Step 9 only in its final sentence; the preceding reasoning shows that any magnitude which measures both AB and CD measures AF. Hence, if a magnitude measures two magnitudes, it also measures their greatest common measure.
